data.title: The Franks negotiate with the Moravians – diplomacy in the age of Great Moravia
data.excerpt: Diplomacy is as old as the first states of early antiquity, and the Slavs of this territory also used it in their dealings with the Frankish Empire — from the envoys of King Dagobert sent to Samo's Empire to the Frankish embassies of the 9th century. The Annals of Fulda show how one such affair got out of the Franks' hands: in 884 Svatopluk laid waste the greater part of Pannonia with fire and sword.
data.metaTitle: The Franks negotiate with the Moravians
data.metaDescription: Diplomacy between the Franks and the Moravians, from Fredegar to the Annals of Fulda, with a period account of the catastrophe that struck Pannonia in 884.

children.text: Diplomacy has existed at least since the time when the first states were coming into being in early antiquity, and it has its roots in the first civilisations. The first signs of diplomacy appeared already in antiquity: as early as the third millennium BC the Egyptian rulers were attempting to establish contacts with neighbouring countries. In the second millennium BC Egypt was already maintaining lively trading, cultural and political relations with the whole of the then known world — with the state of the Hittites in Western Asia, with the Mesopotamian states (Mitanni, Babylon, Assyria), with the Cretan kingdom and the islands of the Aegean Sea, and with the Syrian and Palestinian princes.

blocks.text: A great catastrophe then struck Pannonia. Let us show how it all began. When, therefore, the two brothers Wilhelm and Engilschalk administered, by the commission of King Louis the Elder, the frontier march of the kingdom of the Bavarians in the east against the Moravians, they are said to have exerted themselves very little in the fighting for the defence of the homeland. They continued to be little active, and when at last they also completed the final days of their lives, the sons of these brothers did not obtain their offices, but the king appointed count Aribo as administrator. The sons of these men and their kinsmen interpreted this circumstance as an expression of hostility. They declared that one of two things must happen: either count Aribo would die, if he did not give up the office belonging to their fathers, or they themselves would die by the edge of the sword. Aribo, alarmed by this news, entered into friendly contacts with Svatopluk, duke of the nation of the Moravians. He did not even hesitate to give his own son as a hostage in order to strengthen the treaties concluded. Meanwhile the said youths turned to certain Bavarian magnates with a request for advice. Then they gathered their kinsmen and military units from all sides, and so succeeded in assembling a strong army. With its help they drove out, without any respect, the count whom the king had appointed to the office, and themselves seized this territory (the march). This, then, happened after the death of King Louis and of his sons Carloman and Louis. Their successor in the kingship then became the youngest of the brothers (Charles III the Fat). Shortly afterwards he returned the aforementioned march to Aribo, who had held it before. In connection with this fact Pannonia experienced, as we have already mentioned, a catastrophe, and how it came about we shall relate, for the refreshment of the reader, by means of a quatrain inserted into the prose:

children.text: From the history of the Slavs in the territory of present-day Slovakia we know that many disputes between them and the Frankish Empire were settled, or attempts were made to settle them, by diplomatic means. The
Chronicle of Fredegar

already describes the well-known scene in which the envoys of King Dagobert went to “settle” the dispute with Samo's Empire, which had arisen from the alleged killing of Frankish merchants by the Slavs.   
  The scene which our collaborator Tomáš Humaj drew for our site relates to a later period (the 9th century) and represents a depiction of diplomatic negotiations between Frankish envoys and the prince (or king?) of Great Moravia, whom they had come to ask for military help.
One of such situations (which, however, subsequently got somewhat out of the Franks' hands) is described for us by the Annals of Fulda.
The year 884.
“Every kingdom – says Jesus – that is divided against itself
becomes unsteady, nor does anything discordant have permanence.
Therefore, most beautiful land, plots and afflictions pursue you,
therefore, once happy Pannonia, torment pursues you.”
In that year, then, when the said youths brought it about that
count Aribo was deprived of the office entrusted to him by the king,
Svatopluk, duke of the Moravians

, with a head full of stratagems and cunning, did not forget how much hardship he had had to suffer together with his people at the hands of the forebears of these youths, in the times when the frontier territory (the march) of the Bavarians had spread as far as them (the Moravians). Since
he also bore in mind the friendship and the oath given to Aribo, he set out with an army to avenge everything

, and in this he also succeeded. On the northern side of the Danube he captured the middle one of Engilschalk's three sons, Verinhar, and count Vezzil, who was their kinsman, and had their right hands and their tongues cut off. Besides this, however – it is horror to think of it – they also deprived them of their private parts, or genitals, in such a way that not a trace of them remained. Some others of their people they sent back without their right or left hand. At the duke's command the army gave everything over to the flames. Besides this they also sent scouts beyond the Danube, and wherever any property of the said youths was to be found, they burned it at once.

These shameful deeds, brought about by the imprudent conduct of the youths, went on throughout the whole year. Since the youths hoped for nothing good from the king on account of their offence against Aribo, they fled and entered the service of Carloman's son Arnulf, who at that time administered Pannonia. When duke Svatopluk heard of this, he sent envoys to him and gave him this message: “Your men are plotting against my life and are joining with the Bulgarians against my kingdom” (for they had laid waste his kingdom in the preceding year), “and therefore I wish you to confirm by oath that this is not true.” Arnulf sent him word that he would do no such thing.

Shortly afterwards the duke assembled very numerous military units from all the Slavic lands and invaded Pannonia with them. He killed furiously and bloodily like a wolf and laid waste the greater part of it with fire and sword. He overturned and destroyed everything, and therefore this catastrophe may with full right be described in verse:
“This is the lament of the homeland, and at the same time its sorrowful funeral.”
When the suffering caused by the said youthful imprudence came to an end, after the passage of one year the duke returned home together with his army without losses.
